(p-316) Surah al-Anfal

It is Medinan by consensus (ijma'). Al-Mawardi reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it contains seven Meccan verses, the first of which is: ﴿And [remember] when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ [al-Anfal 8:30].

﴿They ask you about the spoils of war. Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger. So fear Allah, set right your relations with one another, and obey Allah and His Messenger, if you are believers.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the spoils of war﴾ — regarding the occasion of its revelation there are three opinions.

The first: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said on the day of Badr: 'Whoever kills a slain enemy, for him is such-and-such, and whoever takes a captive, for him is such-and-such.' The elders stood firm beneath the banners, but the young men hastened to the killing and the booty. The elders said to the young men: 'Share them with us, for we were a support (ridf) for you'; but they refused, so they disputed before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the surah of [al-Anfal] was revealed." Narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-317) The second: "Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas took a sword on the day of Badr and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, give it to me.' So this verse was revealed." Narrated by Mus'ab ibn Sa'd from his father. In another narration, "from Sa'd, who said: I killed Sa'd ibn al-'As, took his sword, and brought it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: 'Go and throw it into the pile (al-qabd).' So I returned, with a grief known only to Allah. I had not gone far before the surah of (al-Anfal) was revealed, and he said: 'Go and take your sword.'"

Al-Suddi said: "Sa'd and other men disputed over that sword, so they asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) took it from them, and this verse was revealed."

The third: that the spoils (al-anfal) were exclusively for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and none of them belonged to anyone else, so they asked him to give them some of it, and this verse was revealed. Narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas.

As for the meaning of al-anfal, there are six opinions: (p-318) The first: that they are the spoils of war. Narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, and this was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ata', Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, Abu 'Ubayda, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Qutayba, and others. The singular of al-anfal is nafl. Labid said:

"Indeed, the fear of our Lord is the best nafl,
and by Allah's permission, my delay and my haste."

The second: that they are what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) granted (nafala) to the killer, namely the spoils (salab) of the one he killed.

The third: that they are whatever of the polytheists came over to the Muslims without fighting, whether a slave or an animal, said by 'Ata'. This and the preceding one are both reported from Ibn 'Abbas as well.

The fourth: that it is the one-fifth (khums) which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took from the spoils, said by Mujahid.

The fifth: that it is the extra portions of the raiding parties (anfal al-saraya), said by 'Ali ibn Salih ibn Hayy. It is reported from al-Hasan who said: they are the raiding parties that go forth before the armies.

The sixth: that they are additional allotments which the imam gives to some of the army according to what he sees as beneficial, mentioned by al-Mawardi. Regarding "'an" (about) there are two views.

One: that it is superfluous, and the meaning is "they ask you for the spoils." Thus Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and Abu al-'Aliya read: "yas'alunaka al-anfal," with "'an" omitted.

The second: that it is original, and the meaning is "they ask you about the spoils: to whom do they belong?" or "about the ruling on the spoils." We have already mentioned in the occasion of revelation what relates to both views. It is mentioned that they asked about its ruling because it had been forbidden to the nations before them.

(p-319) * Section

The scholars of abrogation (naskh) and the abrogated differed regarding this verse. Some said: it is abrogating in one respect and abrogated in another, because spoils had been forbidden in the laws of the earlier prophets; Allah abrogated that by this verse, and placed the matter of the spoils under what the Messenger (ﷺ) saw fit. Then that was abrogated by His saying: ﴿And know that whatever you gain of any spoil, a fifth of it belongs to Allah﴾ [al-Anfal 8:41]. Others said: al-anfal refers to two things.

The first: what the Messenger (ﷺ) gives to a group of the bravest and foremost of the army, to draw out their sincere counsel and to urge them to fight.

The second: what remains of the spoils after their division, as narrated from Ibn 'Umar who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent us on a raiding expedition, and we gained camels; each one of us received twelve camels, and we were given an extra camel each. According to this, the ruling is muhkam (firm), because this ruling remains until our time."

Section

It is permissible to grant an extra portion (nafl) before the booty is secured, which is that the imam says: "Whoever takes anything, it is his," and this is the view of the majority. As for after it is secured, there are two narrations from Ahmad. Is the killer entitled to the spoils (salab) of the one he killed if the imam did not stipulate it for him? There are two views.

One: he is entitled to it, said by al-Awza'i, al-Layth, and al-Shafi'i.

The second: he is not entitled to it, and it becomes booty for the army, said by Abu Hanifa and Malik; and there are two narrations from Ahmad corresponding to the two views. (p-320)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾ — they judge concerning them as they wish. ﴿So fear Allah﴾ by abstaining from disobeying Him. ﴿And set right your relations with one another﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "dhat baynikum" is the reality of your connection; al-bayn is the connection, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, your bonds have been severed among you﴾ [al-An'am 6:94].

Then regarding the meaning of the phrase there are two views. One: that the strong should return to the weak, said by 'Ata'. The second: abandoning dispute in submission to Allah and His Messenger.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ — that is: accept what you have been commanded regarding the spoils and other matters.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the believers are those who, when Allah is mentioned﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: when you mention His greatness, His power, and what He has threatened with respect to those who disobey Him, their hearts become frightened. The poet said:

؎ By your life, I do not know, and indeed I am fearful over which of us death will reach first.

It is said: wajila (وَجِلَ) yawjalu (يَوْجَلُ), and also yayjalu (يَيْجَلُ) and yiyjalu (يِيجَلُ). These are four dialects which Sibawayh related, and the best of them is yawjalu. Al-Suddi said: it is the man who intends an act of disobedience, then he remembers Allah and refrains from it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when His verses are recited to them﴾, meaning: the verses of the Qur'an.

Regarding His saying: ﴿it increases them in faith﴾, there are three opinions.

One: (it increases them in) assent (taṣdīq), related by Ibn Abbas. The meaning is that whenever something from Allah comes to them, they believe in it, and so their faith increases with the increase of the verses.

The second: (it increases them in) certainty (yaqīn), related by al-Dahhak.

The third: (it increases them in) fear of Allah (khashyat Allah), related by al-Rabi' ibn Anas. (p-321) We have already mentioned the meaning of tawakkul (trust in Allah, tawakkul) in (Al 'Imran: 122).

Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 8, verse 3:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who establish the prayer﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: this means the five daily prayers. ﴿And from what We have provided them they spend﴾: this means the zakat (obligatory almsgiving).

ALLAH's words: ﴿Those are the true believers.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: "ḥaqqan" (truly) is in the accusative because of a meaning implied by the sentence, and the sentence is ﴿Those are the believers﴾. So the meaning is: "I affirm that as a truth." Muqatil said: the meaning is: ﴿Those are the believers,﴾ there being no doubt about their faith, unlike the doubt of the hypocrites.

ALLAH's words: ﴿For them are degrees with their Lord﴾. ʿAtaʾ said: these are the degrees of Paradise which they ascend by their deeds, and "the generous provision" is what He has prepared for them therein.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 8, verses 5–6:**

Regarding His words, ﴿As your Lord brought you forth﴾, there are five opinions about what this *kaf* (the "as" in "as your Lord") is connected to.

The first is that it is connected to *al-Anfal* (the spoils, or the bounties). There are then three opinions about the meaning of the statement:
1. Its interpretation is: "Proceed with God's command concerning the spoils, even if they dislike it, just as you proceeded in your departure from your house while they were averse." This is the view of al-Farra'.
2. The spoils belong to God and the Messenger ﷺ by the binding truth, just as your Lord brought you forth with the truth, even if they dislike that. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.
3. The meaning is: they ask you about the spoils in dispute, just as they disputed with you concerning your departure. This was related by a group of the exegetes.

The second is that it is connected to His words: ﴿So fear God and set right what is between you﴾. The meaning is: piety and reconciliation are good for you, just as God's bringing forth His Prophet Muhammad was good for you, even if some of you disliked it. This is the view of Ikrima.

The third is that it is connected to His words: ﴿they dispute with you﴾. The meaning is: their disputing with you over the spoils is like God's bringing you forth to Badr while they were averse. This is the view of al-Kisa'i.

The fourth is that it is connected to His words: ﴿Those are the believers in truth﴾. The meaning is: they are truly believers, just as your Lord brought you forth from your house with the truth. This was mentioned by some of the transmitters of the tafsir.

The fifth is that the *kaf* is in the position of an oath (*qasam*, an oath formula), meaning: "By He who brought you forth from your house." This is the view of Abu 'Ubayda, who argued that *ma* is in the position of *alladhi* ("he who"), and from it is His words: ﴿and by Him who created the male and the female﴾ [al-Layl: 3]. Ibn al-Anbari said: this opinion is weak, because the *kaf* is not one of the particles of swearing.

Concerning this bringing forth, there are two opinions:
- One is that it was his departure to Badr, and a group of his Companions disliked it, because they knew they would not gain the spoils except through fighting.
- The other is that it was his departure from Makkah to Madinah, for the Hijrah.

Concerning His words "with the truth," there are two opinions:
- One is that you went out while the truth was with you.
- The other is that you went out with the truth that was obligatory upon you.

Concerning His words: ﴿And indeed a party of the believers were averse﴾, there are two opinions:
- One is that they were averse to your departure.
- The other is that they were averse to the diversion of the spoils away from them. This was the aversion of natural inclination, due to the hardship of the journey and the fighting, and not an aversion to God's command.

His words: ﴿They dispute with you concerning the truth﴾ mean: concerning the fighting on the day of Badr. This is because they went out without preparation, so they said: "Why did you not inform us of the fighting so that we could take our provisions?" So they argued with him, seeking a concession to abandon the fighting.

Concerning His words: ﴿after it has become clear﴾, there are three opinions:
1. Its obligation became clear to them.
2. Its correctness became clear to them.
3. It became clear to them that you do only what you are commanded to do.

Concerning "those who dispute," there are two opinions:
- One is that they are a group of the Muslims. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the view of the majority.
- The other is that they are the polytheists. This was said by Ibn Zayd. According to this, their disputing concerns the truth, which is monotheism, and not the fighting.

According to the first opinion, the meaning of His words ﴿as though they were being driven to death﴾ is: in meeting the enemy, ﴿while they were looking on﴾, because the most severe condition of one who is driven to death is that he is looking at it and knows it. According to the view of Ibn Zayd: it is as though they were being driven to death when they were invited to Islam, because of their aversion to it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 7–8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Allah promised you one of the two groups﴾. The people of tafsir said: "Abu Sufyan came from al-Sham with a caravan belonging to Quraysh. When he drew near Badr, Jibril descended and informed the Prophet ﷺ of that, so he went out with a group of his companions, intending them. They informed Quraysh of that, so they sent ʿAmr ibn Ḍamḍam al-Ghifari to Makkah seeking aid. Quraysh went out to protect the caravan. Abu Sufyan veered off along the seashore and escaped, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was thwarted. Jibril then descended with this verse: ﴿And when Allah promised you﴾." The meaning: remember when Allah promised you one of the two groups. The two groups were: Abu Sufyan and the wealth that was with him, and Abu Jahl and those with him from Quraysh. When Abu Sufyan got away with what he had, he wrote to Quraysh: "If you went out to protect your camels, I have already secured them for you." Abu Jahl said: "By Allah, we will not return." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out intending the people, and his companions disliked that and wished that they might obtain the group that had the spoils without fighting. This is His saying: ﴿and you wished that the one without the thorn [of arms] would be yours﴾, that is, the one without weapons. It is said: "So-and-so is shaki al-silah" (lightly pronounced), and "shakk fi al-silah" (with shadda), and "shaʾik." Abu ʿUbayda said: the figurative sense of shawka is sharpness/edge; one says, "How strong is the shawka of the Banu so-and-so," meaning their edge. Al-Akhfash said: he made "dhat al-shawka" feminine only because it refers to the group (ṭaʾifa).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah intended to establish the truth﴾. Regarding what is meant by "the truth" there are two opinions.

The first: it is Islam, said by Ibn ʿAbbas and others.

The second: it is the Qur'an, and the meaning is: what was revealed to you of the Qur'an becomes established.

His saying, exalted is He: "by His words", that is, by His promises that preceded concerning the exaltation of the religion, like His saying: ﴿that He may make it prevail over all religion﴾ [al-Tawba: 33].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and cut off the last remnant of the disbelievers﴾, that is, uproot their root. We have explained this in (al-Anʿam: 45).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that He might establish the truth﴾. The meaning: and He intends to cut off the last remnant of the disbelievers so that the truth may be established. Regarding this truth, the two opinions mentioned earlier apply. As for falsehood, it is shirk; and "the criminals" here are the polytheists.

[p. 325] His saying, Exalted is He: "Idh" (when). Ibn Jarir said: it is connected to "yubtil" (He nullifies). Regarding His saying ﴿tastaghithuna﴾ (you cried for help), there are two opinions.

One is: you seek victory (tastansirun). The second is: you seek protection (tastajirun). The difference between them is that one who seeks victory (al-mustansir) asks for triumph, while one who seeks protection (al-mustajir) asks for deliverance.

Regarding the ones who cried for help (al-mustaghithin), there are two opinions.

One is that they were the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Muslims; this was said by al-Zuhri.

The second is that they were the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; this was said by al-Suddi. As for the reinforcement (al-imdad), it was already discussed in [Al 'Imran 3:124]. His saying "bi-alf" (with a thousand): al-Dahhak and Abu Raja' recited it as "bi-alaf" (with thousands), with a hamza that is elongated and an alif, in the plural form. Abu al-'Aliyya and Abu al-Mutawakkil recited "bi-uluf" (with thousands), with a raised hamza and lam and a waw after them, in the plural form. Ibn Hadhlam and al-Jahdari recited "bi-ulf" (with a thousand), with the alif and lam vowelled with a damma and without a waw or an alif. Abu al-Jawza' and Abu 'Imran recited "bi-yalf" (with a thousand), with a fathah on the ya' and a sukun on the lam, without a waw or an alif.

As for His saying ﴿mut'dhifin﴾ (following one another / coming in succession), Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "mur'difin" with a kasra on the dal. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and al-Farra' said: they are those who come in succession. Abu 'Ali said: it may have two meanings.

One is that they were "mur'dafin" like them (i.e., made to follow them as riders behind them). You say: "I made Zayd ride behind me on my mount," so the second object is omitted in the verse.

The second is that they came after them. The Arabs say: "The Banu so-and-so are our successors (murdufununa)," meaning: they come after us. Abu 'Ubayda said: "murdafin" means they came after. Nafi' and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited "mur'dafin" with a fathah on the dal. Al-Farra' said: he meant: He did this to them, that is, Allah made the Muslims follow them (with reinforcements). Mu'adh al-Qari, Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji and Abu Mijlaz recited "mur'addafin" with a fathah on the ra' and the dal, with a shadda. Abu al-Jawza' and Abu 'Imran recited "murudifin" with a damma on the ra' and a kasra on the dal. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said "radafa al-rajul" when you ride behind a man, and "ardaftuhu" when you make him ride behind you. It is said: "hadhihi dabbatun la turadifu" (this is a mount that does not carry a rider behind), and it is not said "la turdifu." It is also said: "ardafat al-rajul" when you come after him. So the meaning of "mur'difin" is that they come in one group after another group. In the language it is permissible to say: "murad'difin," "murudd'difin" and "muridd'difin." The dal is always kasra and shadda, while the ra' may be read with a fathah, a damma or a kasra.

[p. 327] Sibawayh said: the original form is "murtadifin," then the ta' was assimilated into the dal, becoming "muraddifin," because you transferred the vowel of the ta' onto the ra'. If you wish, you do not transfer the vowel of the ta' and you give the ra' a kasra because of the meeting of two sukuns. Those who vowelled the ra' with a damma made it follow the damma of the mim. The explanation of His saying ﴿وَما جَعَلَهُ اللَّهُ إلا بُشْرى﴾ (And Allah did not make it except as good news) [Al 'Imran 3:126] has already been given in (Al 'Imran). The words of the Most High: "When He covered you with drowsiness as a security from Him." It is also possible that the meaning is: "Remember when drowsiness covered you."

Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr recited "إذْ يَغْشاكُمْ" (yaghshakum) with a fatha on the ya, a jazm on the ghayn, a fatha on the shin, and an alif, with "al-nu'as" (drowsiness) in the nominative case. Asim, Ibn Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i recited "يُغَشِّيكُمْ" (yughashshikum) with a damma on the ya, a fatha on the ghayn, a shadda on the shin with a kasra, and "al-nu'as" in the accusative case. Nafi' recited "يُغْشِيكُمْ" (yughshikum) with a damma on the ya, a jazm on the ghayn, a kasra on the shin, and "al-nu'as" in the accusative case.

Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi (a scholar of Damascus) said: the sentence refers back to the words ﴿وَلِتَطْمَئِنَّ بِهِ قُلُوبُكُمْ﴾ ("and that your hearts may be assured by it"), namely "when drowsiness covered you."

Al-Zajjaj said: "wa-amanatan" (as a security) is in the accusative case as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), like your saying: "I did that out of fear of evil." It is said: "amina," "amina amnan," "amanan," and "amanatan." Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Aliyah, Ibn Yamur, and Ibn Muhaysin recited "أمَنَةً مِنْهُ" (amnatan minhu) with a sukun on the mim.

The words of the Most High: ﴿وَيُنَزِّلُ عَلَيْكم مِنَ السَّماءِ ماءً﴾ ("and He sends down upon you water from the sky"). Ibn Abbas said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) camped on the day of Badr, and between him and the water there was a stretch of sand. The polytheists overpowered them at the water, and the Muslims were afflicted with thirst. They began to pray while in a state of impurity (muhdithin). Satan cast whispering into their hearts, saying: 'You claim that you are the friends of Allah and His Messenger is among you, yet the polytheists have overpowered you at the water, and you pray in a state of impurity.' So Allah sent down rain upon them, and they drank and purified themselves. Ibn Zayd said: "rijz al-shaytan" (the defilement of Satan) is his scheming, in that he put into their hearts that you have no strength against these people.

Ibn al-Anbari said: the lack of water distressed them, since they were in need of it, so Allah sent the rain. Thus the whispering of Satan, which earns the punishment and anger of Allah, went away, since "rijz" means punishment.

The words of the Most High: ﴿وَلِيَرْبِطَ عَلى قُلُوبِكُمْ﴾ ("and that He may bind upon your hearts"). "Al-rabt" (binding) means tightening. The second is that it refers to the binding (al-rabt). The meaning is: "and He makes the feet firm by the binding." This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The second: "Give them good news of victory." So the king (angel) would walk in front of the rows in the form of a man, saying: "Rejoice, for God is your helper." This was said by Muqatil.

The third: "Strengthen them with things you cast into their hearts, by which they will be made firm." This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: "Set their resolve and intentions right toward jihad." This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi. As for *al-Ru'b* (terror), it is fear. Al-Sa'ib ibn Yasar said: "Whenever we asked Yazid ibn 'Amir al-Siwa'i about the terror which God cast into the hearts of the polytheists, how was it? His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So strike above the necks﴾. Concerning the addressees of this there are two opinions.

One of them: they are the angels. Ibn al-Anbari said: "The angels did not know where to aim the strike on people, so God taught them that."

(p. 330) The second: they are the believers. This was mentioned by a group of the exegetes. And concerning the meaning of the statement there are two opinions.

One of them: "Strike the necks," and "above" is a *silah* (a particle serving only to complete the sense, without independent meaning). Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verses 15–16:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When you meet those who disbelieve advancing (zahfan)﴾. Al-zahf (a massed body advancing) is a group that advances toward its enemy; so said al-Layth. Al-tazahuf (drawing near and converging) means approaching one another, as al-A'sha said:

"For whom are the litters, whose going advances (tazhafu)?"

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the speech is: when you confront them for battle, then do not turn your backs, and whoever turns his back to them on the day of their battle, ﴿except one who swerves (mutaharrifan) to fight, or withdraws (mutahayyizan) to a company﴾. It is also permissible that their accusative be in the sense of an exception (istithnā'), so the meaning becomes: except a man who swerves or withdraws. The original form of mutahayyiz is mutaḥyawiz, and the yā' was assimilated into the wāw.

This is the meaning of the saying of Mujahid.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 8, verses 19–20:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If you seek a decision﴾. Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are five views.

The first: The Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked God for victory and requested of Him triumph, and so this verse was revealed. This meaning is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ata al-Khurasani. (p-335)

The second: Abu Jahl said, "O God, whichever of us is more beloved to You and more pleasing in Your sight, then give him victory today." So this verse was revealed. Abu Salih narrated this from Ibn Abbas.

The third: The polytheists took hold of the curtains of the Ka'bah before they set out for Badr, and said, "O God, grant victory to the higher of the two armies and the nobler of the two tribes." So this verse was revealed. Al-Suddi said this.

The fourth: The polytheists said, "O God, we do not know what Muhammad has brought, so decide between us and him with truth." So this verse was revealed. Ikrimah said this.

The fifth: They said in Makkah, ﴿O God, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal 8:32], and so they were punished on the day of Badr. Ibn Zayd said this.

From these views it follows that regarding those addressed in His saying, "If you seek...", there are two opinions.

One: They are the believers. Two: They are the polytheists, and this is the more well-known view.

Regarding the meaning of istiftah (seeking an opening, i.e. seeking victory or a decision), there are two views.

One: It means seeking victory (istinsar). This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Zajjaj, among others. If we say they are the Muslims, the meaning is: "If you seek victory, then victory has come to you through the angels." If we say they are the polytheists, it admits two readings. One: "If you seek victory, then victory has come against you." The second: "If you seek victory for the more beloved of the two groups to God, then victory has come for the more beloved of the two groups."

The second: Istiftah means seeking judgment (talab al-hukm). The meaning is: "If you ask for a judgment between you and the Muslims, then the judgment has come to you." This is the view taken by Ikrimah, Mujahid, and Qatadah. As for His saying, ﴿And if you desist, it is better for you﴾, it is addressed to the polytheists according to the consensus of the group.

Regarding its meaning there are two views.

One: "If you desist from fighting Muhammad (ﷺ) and from disbelief." This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. (p-336)

The second: "If you desist from your seeking of victory, it is better for you, because it was against you, not for you." This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Regarding His saying, ﴿And if you return, We will return﴾, there are two views.

One: "If you return to fighting, We will return to your defeat." This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. The second: "If you return to seeking victory, We will return to granting victory to Muhammad (ﷺ)." This was said by al-Suddi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And your company will not avail you anything at all﴾, meaning your group, even if it is large, ﴿and that God is with the believers﴾ by aid and victory. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Hamzah, and Abu Bakr from Asim read "wa-inna Allah" with a kasrah on the alif (wa-inna, i.e., beginning a new clause). Nafi', Ibn Amir, and Hafs from Asim read "wa-anna" with a fathah on the alif (wa-anna, i.e., "and that", linked grammatically to what precedes). Whoever reads with a kasrah on "inna" begins a new sentence. Al-Farra' said: "This is more beloved to me than the fathah." Whoever reads with a fathah intends: "and because God is with the believers."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not turn away from Him﴾ has two views.

One: Do not turn away from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

The second: Do not turn away from the command of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), ﴿while you hear﴾ what has been revealed of the Qur'an. Both views are narrated from Ibn Abbas.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 21–22:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not be like those who say, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ — the scholars differed concerning whom it was revealed about, in three opinions.

The first: that it was revealed concerning the Banu Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy. This was said by Abu Salih, on the authority of Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it concerns the Jews, the Banu Qurayzah and the Banu al-Nadir. This was also related from Ibn Abbas.

The third: that it concerns the hypocrites. This was said by Ibn Ishaq, al-Waqidi, and Muqatil.

As for the meaning of the statement, there are two views.

One of them: they said, "We hear," but they did not reflect upon what they heard, so they were like one who did not hear. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: they said, "We hear," the hearing of one who accepts, but they were not like that. This was related from Muqatil.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the worst of living beings in the sight of Allah are the deaf and the dumb﴾ — the scholars differed concerning whom it was revealed about, in two views.

One of them: it was revealed concerning the Banu Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy. This was said by Abu Salih, on the authority of Ibn Abbas.

The second: it concerns the hypocrites. This was said by Ibn Ishaq and al-Waqidi. The "dawabb" (living creatures that crawl or move on the earth) is the name for every living animal that crawls; and we have already explained in Surah al-Baqarah (2:18) the meaning of "deaf" and "dumb," and why He named them thus.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 23:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them﴾ — concerning this there are four opinions.

The first: "If He had known in them truthfulness and submission (Islam)." The second: "If He had known in them good in the prior decree (al-qada' al-sabiq)." The third: "If He had known that they would reform." The fourth: "If He had known that they would lend an ear (yusghun)."

Concerning His words: ﴿He would have made them hear﴾ there are three opinions. The first: "He would have made them hear the answer to every question they asked about," related by al-Zajjaj. The second: "He would have granted them understanding," related by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The third: "He would have made them hear the speech of the dead, who would testify to your prophethood," related by al-Mawardi. Concerning His words: ﴿while they turn away, being averse﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: "They are deniers," related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: "They turn away from what He made them hear, out of their obstinacy," related by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 24:

Allah's words ﴿Respond﴾ mean: answer.

Allah's words ﴿when He calls you﴾ refer to the Messenger, ﴿to that which gives you life﴾. On this phrase there are six opinions.

The first is that "that which gives you life" is everything the Messenger calls to. This is the view of Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas. In the single narrations of al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, he said: "I was praying in the mosque, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called me, but I did not answer him. Then I came to him and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, I was praying.' He said, 'Did not Allah say: Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life?' I said, 'Yes, and I will not do it again, if Allah wills.'"

The second is that it is the truth. This was transmitted by Shibl, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid.

The third is that it is faith. This was transmitted by Warqa', from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, and al-Suddi also said this.

The fourth is that it is following the Qur'an. This was said by Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

The fifth is that it is jihad. This was said by Ibn Ishaq. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is the jihad which gives life to their religion and raises it.

The sixth is that it is the revival of their affairs. This was said by al-Farra'. Thus, regarding their "life," there are five opinions.

The first is that it is the setting right of their affairs in this world and the Hereafter.

The second is the lasting of a good remembrance for them in this world, and eternal life in the Hereafter.

The third is the continuance of their bliss in the Hereafter.

The fourth is their being believers, because the disbeliever is like the dead.

The fifth is that He gives them life after their death. This is according to the view of those who said it is jihad, because the martyrs are alive, and because jihad restores their honour after their humiliation, so it is as if they have become living through it.

Allah's words ﴿And know that Allah comes between a man and his heart﴾. On this phrase there are ten opinions.

The first is that He comes between the believer and disbelief, and between the disbeliever and faith. This was transmitted by Ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said this.

The second is that He comes between the believer and his sin, and between the disbeliever and his obedience. This was transmitted by al-Awfi, from Ibn Abbas, and al-Dahhak and al-Farra' also said this.

The third is that He comes between a man and his heart so that He does not let it understand. This was said by Mujahid. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is that He comes between a man and his intellect, so hasten to good deeds, for you are not safe from the loss of your intellects, and then you will not attain what you have sent ahead.

The fourth is that the meaning is: He is near to a man, nothing of his secret is hidden from Him, as in His words ﴿And We are nearer to him than his jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16]. This is the meaning of Qatadah's view.

The fifth is that He comes between a man and his heart, so that he cannot have faith or disbelief except by His permission. This was said by al-Suddi.

The sixth is that He comes between a man and his desire. Ibn Qutaybah mentioned this.

The seventh is that He comes between a man and what he wishes in his heart, such as long life, victory, and other things.

The eighth is that He comes between a man and his heart by death, so hasten to good deeds before it happens.

The ninth is that He comes between a man and his heart by his deed, so that the servant does not conceal anything within himself without Allah knowing it, and He cannot be made absent from it.

The tenth is that He comes between what He places in the heart of fear or security, so that one becomes secure after fear, and fearful after security. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned the meaning of these opinions.

Al-Zajjaj related that when they reflected on the great number of their enemy and the smallness of their own number, so that fear entered their hearts, Allah the Exalted informed them that He comes between a man and his heart by replacing fear with security, and replacing the strength of their enemy with weakness. This verse makes clear that Allah the Exalted is the One who turns the hearts and disposes of them.

Allah's words ﴿And that to Him you will be gathered﴾, that is: for the recompense for your deeds.

(p-341) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And beware of a trial﴾. The scholars differed concerning who it was revealed about, in four opinions.

One: it was revealed specifically about the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak. Al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam said: "We recited it for a time, and we did not think we were among its people, so then we were the ones meant by it."

The second: it was revealed about two men from Quraysh. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas, but he did not name them.

The third: it is general. Ibn Abi Talha related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "In this verse, God commanded the believers not to allow the reprehensible among them, lest God afflict them all with punishment." Mujahid said: "This verse is for you as well."

The fourth: it was revealed about ʿAli, ʿAmmar, Talha and al-Zubayr. This was said by al-Hasan. Al-Suddi said: it was revealed specifically about the people of Badr, and it befell them on the Day of the Camel.

Regarding the word "trial" (fitnah) here, there are seven opinions.

One: fighting. The second: misguidance. The third: silence about denouncing what is reprehensible. The fourth: testing. The fifth: trial through wealth and children. The sixth: affliction. The seventh: the appearance of innovations (bida').

As for His saying: ﴿Smite not those who have done wrong among you in particular﴾, al-Farra' said: He commanded them, then forbade them, and in it is a trace of the conditional. Even though it is a prohibition, like His saying: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his hosts crush you﴾ [al-Naml: 18], He commanded them, then forbade them; and in it is the interpretation of the conditional. Al-Akhfash said: "Lā tuṣībanna" is not an answer, but rather it is a prohibition following a prohibition (p-342); and if it were an answer, the nun (nūn) would not have entered. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two opinions concerning it.

One of them: that the statement is to be interpreted as a report, since the meaning is: if you do not guard against it, it will strike those who have done wrong, and others besides them; that is, it does not fall only upon the wrongdoers without others, but it falls upon both the righteous and the wicked. Then, when the verb appeared in the manner of a prohibition, and the prohibition returns to the sense of a command (since the speaker says "Do not stand," meaning "Abandon standing"), it came with this as an answer to the command, or as something like an answer to it, and so a sense of prohibition was emphasized for it, and the nun entered, as is well known in the case of the prohibition and what resembles it.

The second: that it is a pure prohibition, its meaning being: let not the wrongdoers intend this trial, lest they perish; so the nun entered to emphasize the future, as in His saying: "lā yaḥṭimannakum." The commentators have two opinions regarding the meaning of the statement.

One of them: "Let not the trial strike those who have done wrong."

The second: "Let not the punishment of the trial strike." If it is said: "What is the sin of one who has not done wrong?" The answer: by his agreement with the wicked, or by his silence about denouncing, or by his abandoning flight, he deserves the punishment. ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb recited "la-tuṣībanna alladhīna ẓalamū" without an alif.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 26:

One opinion is that they were the people of Mecca. This is said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second is that they were Persia and the Romans; this is said by Wahb ibn Munabbih. The third is that they were the polytheists who attended Badr, while the Muslims were few on that day; this is said by Qatadah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So He sheltered you﴾, has two opinions.

One of them: He sheltered you in Medina through the Hijrah (emigration). This is said by Ibn ʿAbbas and most scholars.

The second: He made for you a refuge in which you dwell in security. This is mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And strengthened you with His help﴾, there are two opinions.

One of them: He strengthened you with the angels on the day of Badr. This is said by the majority. The second: He supported you with His help at Badr and other occasions. This is said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And provided for you of the good things﴾, there are two opinions.

One of them: They are the spoils of war which He made lawful for them. This is said by al-Suddi.

The second: They are the good things which He enabled them to have. This is mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Ibn al-Jawzi, *Zad al-Masir*, on Surah 8, verse 27:

God's words: ﴿O you who believe, do not betray God and the Messenger﴾. The scholars differed over who the verse was revealed about, and they gave four opinions.

The first: it was revealed about Abu Lubabah ibn Abd al-Mundhir. The story is that when the Prophet ﷺ besieged Banu Qurayzah, they asked him to make peace with them on the same terms he had made with Banu al-Nadir, namely that they would depart for the land of Syria. He refused to grant them that unless they came down under the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. They refused and said: "Send Abu Lubabah to us," for he was sympathetic to them, because his son and his family were with them. So he sent him to them. They said: "What do you think? Should we come down under the judgment of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh?" Abu Lubabah pointed with his hand to his throat, meaning: it is slaughter, so do not do it. They obeyed him, and that was his betrayal. Abu Lubabah said: "My feet did not move until I knew that I had betrayed God and His Messenger, and this verse was revealed." This is the view of Ibn Abbas and most scholars. It is also reported that Abu Lubabah, after the revelation of this verse, tied himself to one of the pillars of the mosque and said: "By God, I will not taste food or drink until I die or God accepts my repentance." He remained like that for seven days, then God accepted his repentance. He said: "By God, I will not free myself until the Messenger of God ﷺ is the one who frees me." So he came and untied him with his own hand. Abu Lubabah said: "Part of the completion of my repentance is that I abandon the house of my people in which I committed the sin, and that I strip myself of my wealth." The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "A third will suffice for you."

The second: Jibril came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said: "Abu Sufyan is at such and such a place." The Messenger of God ﷺ said to his companions: "Go out to him, and keep it secret." But a man among the hypocrites wrote to him: "Muhammad intends to attack you, so take your precaution." Then this verse was revealed. This was said by Jabir ibn Abdullah.

The third: it was revealed about the killing of Uthman ibn Affan. This was said by al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah.

The fourth: certain people used to hear a saying from the Messenger of God ﷺ and then spread it until it reached the polytheists, so this verse was revealed. This was said by al-Suddi.

Regarding betrayal of God, there are two views. One: abandoning His obligations (fara'id, the duties prescribed by God). The other: disobedience to His Messenger.

Regarding betrayal of the Messenger, there are two views. One: opposing him in private after obeying him in public. The other: abandoning his sunnah (the practice and way he established).

Concerning what is meant by "trusts" (amanat), there are three views.

The first: they are the obligations (fara'id). This was said by Ibn Abbas. Regarding betraying them, there are two views: one, diminishing them; the other, abandoning them.

The second: they are the religion. This was said by Ibn Zayd. The meaning would then be: do not show faith while concealing disbelief.

The third: they are general, covering the betrayal of anyone entrusted with something. The revelation of the verse concerning what happened with Abu Lubabah confirms this.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 28–29:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are but a trial﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: This address was directed to Abu Lubaba, because he had wealth and children among the Banu Qurayza. As for the trial (fitna), what is meant by it is the testing and examination which reveals what is in the soul of pursuing desire or avoiding it, ﴿and that with Allah is a great reward﴾, which is better than wealth and children. (p-346)

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿If you fear Allah﴾, that is, by abandoning His disobedience and avoiding betrayal of Allah and His Messenger.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿He will grant you a criterion (furqan)﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions.

The first: that it is a way out. This was transmitted by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿIkrima, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Qutayba also said so. The meaning is: He will grant you a way out in your religion from misguidance.

The second: that it is deliverance. This was transmitted by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Qatada and al-Suddi also said so.

The third: that it is victory. This was transmitted by al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Farra' also said so.

The fourth: that it is guidance in their hearts by which they distinguish between truth and falsehood. This was said by Ibn Zayd and Ibn Ishaq.
