Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 30:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾. This verse is connected to His saying: ﴿And remember when you were few﴾ [al-A'raf: 86]. So the meaning is: remind the believers of what Allah bestowed upon them, and remember when those who disbelieved plotted against you.

Explanation of how they plotted

The people of tafsir said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was given the pledge at the night of al-'Aqabah, and commanded his Companions to join [him] in Medina, Quraysh became fearful that his affair would prevail. They said: 'By Allah, it is as if he has already attacked you with men.' So a group of their nobles gathered to enter Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh) to consult about his affair. Iblis confronted them in the form of an old shaykh. They said: 'Who are you?' He said: 'I am a shaykh from the people of Najd. I heard what you have gathered for, so I wished to attend with you, and you will not lack sincere counsel from my opinion.' They said: 'Enter.' So he entered with them. They said: 'Consider the matter of this man.' Some of them said: 'Bind him in chains, and wait for him to meet the fate of the calamities of time.' Iblis said: 'This is not an opinion. His companions will soon rise and seize him from your hands.' Someone said: 'Expel him from among you.' He said: 'This is not an opinion. He will soon gather [people] against you and then march against you.' Abu Jahl said: 'We take a young man from every tribe, then we give each young man a sword, and they strike him with it as one man strikes, so his blood is spread among the tribes. Then the clan of Banu Hashim will not be able to fight all of Quraysh, and they will accept the blood-money, and we will be relieved.' Iblis said: 'By Allah, this is the opinion.' So they dispersed on that [plan]. Jibril came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), commanded him not to sleep in his bed, and informed him of the plot of the people. So he did not sleep in his bed that night, and he commanded 'Ali to sleep in his place, while the polytheists stood guard over him. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rose in the morning, Allah permitted him to leave for Medina. When the polytheists came in the morning, they saw 'Ali and said: 'Where is your companion?' He said: 'I do not know.' They tracked his trail until they reached the mountain, and they passed by the cave, and they saw the spider's web, and they said: 'Had he entered it, there would not have been a spider's web upon it.'"

As for His saying: ﴿to imprison you﴾, Ibn Qutaybah said: its meaning is: to confine you. It is said: "So-and-so is athbata waja'an (incapacitated by pain)" when he is unable to move. The commentators have two views regarding it. (p-348)

The first: to bind you in chains, said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and others.

The second: to confine you in prison, said by 'Ata' and al-Suddi and others. The people had intended to lock him in a room, bolt its door upon him, and throw food and drink to him. The explanation of plotting has already preceded in [Al 'Imran: 54].

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them﴾. The people of tafsir (exegesis) mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn Alqama ibn Kalada, and that when he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recounting the stories of the earlier generations, he said: "If you wished, you could say the like of this." Regarding His words ﴿We have heard﴾ there are two views.

The first: "We have heard from you, but we will not obey you."

The second: "We have heard the like of this before," for al-Nadr used to travel to Fars (Persia) as a merchant, and he would hear the worshippers reading the Injil (Gospel). The challenge has shown the falsehood of the one who said: ﴿If we wished, we would say the like of this﴾. The meaning of al-asatir (fables) has already been explained in [al-An'am: 25].

The Lord's words: ﴿And when they said, "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You..."﴾ Scholars differed about who said this, and there are three opinions.

The first is that it was revealed concerning an-Nadr [ibn al-Harith] as well. A group related this from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', and as-Suddi also said so.

The second is that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, since he was the one who said this. Anas ibn Malik reported it, and it is narrated in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim).

The third is that it was revealed concerning Quraysh: they said this, then they regretted it and said, "Forgive us, O Allah," so Allah revealed: ﴿But Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾. Abu Ma'shar related this from Yazid ibn Ruman and Muhammad ibn Qays.

As for what is referred to by His words ﴿if this is indeed﴾, there are three opinions.

The first is that it is the Qur'an. The second is that it is everything the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, such as the command to monotheism and other matters. The third is that it is the honouring of Muhammad (ﷺ) with prophethood from among Quraysh.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 33:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾. Regarding what is referred to by "them," there are two views.

The first: they are the people of Makkah. As for the meaning of the statement, there are two views. One: "Allah would not punish them while you remain among them." Ibn 'Abbas said: "No town is punished until its prophet and the believers with him have left it." The second: "Allah would not punish them while you are alive"; this was said by Abu Sulayman.

The second: the ones referred to are the believers, and the meaning is: Allah would not punish the believers with a kind of punishment by which He destroyed those before them while you are alive. This was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Section

al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah said: this verse is abrogated by His saying: ﴿And why should Allah not punish them?﴾ [al-Anfal: 34] (p-350). This is far-fetched, because abrogation (naskh) does not apply to reports (akhbar). Ibn Abza said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was in Makkah, and Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed ﴿But Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾. Then he migrated to Madinah, and Allah revealed ﴿But Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾. The remnant of the Muslims in Makkah were seeking forgiveness, and when they left, Allah revealed ﴿And why should Allah not punish them?﴾. All the statements of the exegetes indicate that His saying ﴿But Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾ is a new statement from Allah, mighty and majestic. It has been narrated from Muhammad ibn Ishaq that he said: this verse is from the speech of the polytheists, who said: "By Allah, Allah will not punish us while we seek forgiveness." So Allah refuted them with His saying: ﴿And why should Allah not punish them?﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾. Regarding the meaning of this statement there are five views.

The first: Allah would not punish the polytheists while among them are those who are destined to believe. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Zajjaj chose it.

The second: Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness from Allah, for they used to say, "Labbayka," and say, "Ghufranaka" (Your forgiveness). This is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, but it is weak, because the forgiveness sought by a polytheist has no effect on acceptance.

The third: Allah would not punish them, meaning the polytheists, while they, meaning the believers among them, seek forgiveness. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas as well, and al-Dahhak and Abu Malik said likewise. Ibn al-Anbari said: they were described with the attribute of some of them, because the believers were among them, so the general was applied to the particular (p-351), as one says: "The people of the mosque killed a man," and "The people of Basra arrested so-and-so," when perhaps only one man did that.

The fourth: Allah would not punish them while among their loins is one who seeks forgiveness from Allah; this was said by Mujahid. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning of punishing them is destroying them. So the meaning is: Allah would not destroy them, and it was already known in His knowledge that they would have descendants who believe in Him and seek His forgiveness. He therefore described them with the attribute of their offspring, and [the offspring] predominated over them, just as some of them predominated over all of them in the answer preceding it.

The fifth: the meaning is: had they sought forgiveness, Allah would not have punished them, but they did not seek forgiveness, so they deserved the punishment. This is like the Arabs saying: "I would not humiliate you while you honor me," meaning: "I would not have humiliated you had you honored me; but since you do not honor me, you deserve my humiliation." To this view went Qatadah and al-Suddi. Ibn al-Anbari said: this is the choice of the linguists. The exegetes mentioned three views regarding the meaning of this seeking of forgiveness.

The first: that it is the well-known seeking of forgiveness, which we have mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that it means prayer; narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, and by Mansur from Mujahid, and al-Dahhak said likewise.

The third: that it means Islam; narrated by Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid, and 'Ikrimah said likewise.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 34:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what [reason] do they have that Allah should not punish them?﴾ This verse permits their punishment, whereas the previous verse negated that. Is the intended meaning of this [the first punishment] or not? There are two opinions on this.

One of them is that it is the first [punishment], except that the first was prevented by two things. One: the Prophet (ﷺ) being among them. Two: the believers who sought forgiveness being among them. So when separation took place through the migration (hijrah), the punishment fell upon the remaining ones on the day of Badr. It was also said: rather, it fell with the conquest of Makkah.

The second: that the two are different, and on this there are two opinions. One of them: the second punishment is the killing of some of them on the day of Badr, while the first was the eradication of all of them; so the first did not occur, because it is known that some of them believed, and some of their offspring embraced Islam, and the second occurred. The second [opinion]: the first punishment is the punishment of this world, and the second is the punishment of the Hereafter; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. So the meaning becomes: Allah would not be punishing the polytheists while they seek forgiveness in this world, and [yet] what reason do they have that Allah should not punish them in the Hereafter?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while they bar [access to] the Sacred Mosque﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: while they bar [people] ﴿from the Sacred Mosque﴾, its [rightful] guardians. There are two opinions regarding the pronoun in His saying: ﴿and they were not its guardians﴾.

One of them: it refers to "the Mosque," and this is the view of the majority. Al-Hasan said: the polytheists said, "We are the guardians of the Sacred Mosque," so Allah refuted them with this.

The second: it refers back to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; this was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Its guardians are only﴾, i.e., its guardians are not ﴿except the righteous (al-muttaqun)﴾, who are free of polytheism and sins; but most of the people of Makkah do not know who has the better claim to the House of Allah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping.﴾ The occasion of its revelation: they used to circle the House, clapping their hands, whistling, and placing their cheeks on the ground, so this verse was revealed. This was related by Ibn ʿUmar. As for al-mukaʾ (whistling), there are two opinions. (p-353) One: it is whistling. This was said by Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Abu ʿUbaydah, al-Zajjaj, and Ibn Qutaybah. Ibn Faris said: it is said, "makā al-ṭāʾir [yamkū] mukāʾan," meaning when the bird whistled. It is also said, "makiyat yaduhu [tamkā] makan," a maqsur form, meaning it became coarse and rough. And it is said, "tamakkā," meaning he performed wudu'. They recited:

Verily you, and oppression on a path, are like one who wipes his hands with the blood of the slain.

Abu Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman was asked about al-mukaʾ, so he joined his palms and began to whistle into them.

The second: it is inserting their fingers into their mouths, mixing that with clapping (al-taṣdiyah) to disrupt Muhammad's (ﷺ) prayer. This was said by Mujahid. Ibn al-Anbari said: the lexicographers deny that al-mukaʾ means inserting the fingers into the mouths; they said it is only whistling. As for al-taṣdiyah, there are two opinions.

One: it is clapping. This was said by Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, and the majority. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said "ṣadā" when one claps his hands. The rajaz poet said:

She withheld a cheek and withdrew from another cheek, and I, from the wonder of love, clap my hands.

Al-gharw means wonder; it is said, "lā gharwa min kadhā," meaning there is no wonder in such a thing.

The second: al-taṣdiyah is their hindering of people from the Sacred House. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr. Ibn Zayd said: it is their hindering people from the path of Allah and His religion. Muqatil claimed that "when the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed in the Masjid al-Haram, two men of the polytheists from the Banu ʿAbd al-Dar would stand (p-354) on his right and whistle, and two men on his left would clap, so the Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer and recitation were disrupted. Allah destroyed them at Badr, and that is His saying: ﴿So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve﴾, meaning in the oneness of Allah."

If it is asked: how did He call the whistling and clapping a prayer?

Concerning this there are two answers, which Ibn al-Anbari mentioned.

One: they made that in place of the prayer. It is well known in the speech of the Arabs that a man says, "I visited ʿAbd Allah, and his rejection became my kindness (ṣila)," meaning he put rejection in the place of kindness. The poet said:

I said to him, "Feed me, O ʿAmim, some dates," so my dates became a cake of dough and a mash.

That is, he put shouting at me in place of dates.

The second: whoever has whistling and clapping as his prayer, then he has no prayer, just as the Arabs say, "Fulan has no fault except generosity," meaning, from his generosity comes his fault, so he has no fault. The poet said:

A youth whose good qualities are complete, except that he is so generous that he leaves no wealth remaining.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 36:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert [people] from the way of Allah﴾ — the scholars differ regarding whom it was revealed about, in three views. (p-355) One: it was revealed concerning the feeders at Badr. They were twelve men who would feed the people with food, each man feeding for one day. They were: ʿUtbah, Shaybah, Munabbih and Nabiyah, the sons of al-Hajjaj, Abu al-Bukhturi, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu Jahl, his brother al-Harith, Hakim ibn Hizam, Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Zamʿah ibn al-Aswad, and al-Harith ibn ʿAmir ibn Nawfal. This is the saying of Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, who hired two thousand of the Ahabish on the Day of Uhud to fight the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, besides those whom he enlisted from the Arabs. This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr. Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan's expenditure on the disbelievers on the Day of Uhud.

The third: it was revealed concerning the people of Badr, and this was the saying of al-Dahhak. As for "the way of Allah," it is the religion of Allah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then it will become a regret for them﴾ — that is, the outcome of their expenditure will be remorse, because they will not prevail.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 37:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "liyamiza" (lightly). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "liyumayyiza" with the doubled letter (shaddah). Both are dialectal forms: mizatuhu and mayyaztuhu (both meaning "I distinguished it"). Regarding the lam of "liyumayyiza" there are two opinions.

One of them: it is connected to His saying "fa-sayunfiquna-ha" (so they will spend it). This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

The second: it is connected to His saying "ila jahannama yuhsharun" (to Hell they will be gathered). This was said by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari. Regarding the meaning of the verse there are three opinions.

The first: that He may distinguish the people of happiness from the people of wretchedness. This was transmitted by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas. As-Suddi and Muqatil said: He distinguishes the believer from the disbeliever.

The second: that He may distinguish the good deed from the wicked deed. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that He may distinguish the good spending in His way from the wicked spending in the way of Satan. This was said by Ibn Zayd and al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and place the wicked one upon another﴾. That is, He gathers some of it on top of other parts of it, and this is His saying: "fa-yarkumahu" (and He piles it up). Al-Zajjaj said: al-rukam is placing some of a thing upon another. It is said: "rakamtu al-shay'a arkumuhu rakman," and al-rukam is the noun. As for the one who said the intended "wicked" is the disbelievers, then they are in the Fire, some upon others. And the one who said it refers to their wealth has two opinions in this.

One of them: that it is thrown into the Fire so that it may punish its owners with it, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿so their foreheads and their sides will be branded with it﴾ [at-Tawbah: 35].

The second: that when they magnified it in the world, He showed them its worthlessness by casting it into the Fire, just as the sun and the moon are cast into the Fire, so that whoever worshipped them may see their humiliation.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 38:

The words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve﴾. It was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan and his companions; this was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas. Regarding the meaning of the verse there are two views. (p-357) The first: if they cease from fighting, what has passed of their warfare will be forgiven them, so they will not be held accountable for it; and if they return to fighting, then the way of the earlier ones has passed, namely the victory of Allah for His allies. It was also said: it refers to the killing of those who were killed on the day of Badr and the taking of captives.

The second: if they cease from disbelief, what has passed of their sin will be forgiven them; and if they return to it, then the way (sunnah) of the earlier nations of past communities has passed, when they were seized with the uprooting punishment. Yahya ibn Mu'adh said concerning this verse: "Indeed, a monotheism that was not unable to demolish the disbelief that preceded it, is not unable to demolish the sin that follows it."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 39:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah⦆ means: shirk (polytheism). Al-Zajjaj said: "Until people are not tested into the fitnah of disbelief," and what points to this is His saying: ﴿and religion entirely belongs to Allah⦆.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But if they cease⦆ means: from disbelief and fighting, ﴿then indeed Allah is Seeing of what they do⦆. Ya'qub (al-Hadrami), except Rawh, recited "taʿmalūna" (ﺗَﻌْﻤَﻠُﻮﻥَ) with the letter tā' (ta), i.e., "what you do."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they turn away﴾, meaning: they turn away from faith and return to fighting.

(p-358) ﴿Then know that Allah is your Protector (mawla)﴾, meaning: your Ally (waliyy) and your Helper. Ibn Qutaybah said: ﴿An excellent Protector﴾, meaning: an excellent Ally, ﴿and an excellent Helper﴾, meaning: an excellent Helper (al-nasir), like qadir and qadir (the same pattern as "capable" and "capable"), and sami' and sami' (the same pattern as "hearing" and "hearer").

The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 8, Verse 41

[p-359] His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And know that whatever you acquire as spoils of war (ghanima) of anything﴾. The scholars differed over whether ghanima and fay' (property taken from the disbelievers without fighting) have the same meaning or differ, on two opinions.

The first opinion is that they differ. There are then two views on this. One is that ghanima is what is seized of the disbelievers' property, and fay' is what is seized of the lands. This was said by Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib. The second is that ghanima is what is taken by force (anwatan), and fay' is what is taken by agreement (sulh). This was said by Sufyan al-Thawri. It was also said: rather, fay' is what was obtained without horses or riders (bikhail wa la rikab) having been used against it, such as 'ushur (tithes on trade), jizya (the poll tax), property from truces (muhadana) and treaties (sulh), and what they fled and left behind.

The second opinion is that they are one and the same, namely everything obtained from the disbelievers. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Al-Zajjaj said: property is of three kinds. What comes to the Muslims from the disbelievers during war, God has named anfal (spoils) and ghana'im. What comes to them from the disbelievers as kharaj (land tax) or jizya, which was not taken in war, He has named fay'. What leaves the property of the Muslims, such as zakat, vows, and expiations, He has named sadaqa. As for His saying ﴿from anything﴾, what is meant by it is everything to which the name "thing" applies. Mujahid said: "even a needle from among the things."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿then to God belongs its fifth (khumusahu)﴾. 'Abd al-Warith narrated it as "khumsahu" with the letter mim vowelless. On the meaning of the phrase there are two views. [p-359 continues] The first is that God's share is an established right that is spent on His house. Abu al-Aliya said: the spoils were brought, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would divide them into five shares, and then he would divide four among the people, and then he would set aside from the fifth share for the Ka'ba. This is a view that Abu al-Aliya is said to have held alone.

The second is that the mention of God here is for one of two reasons. One is that He is the one who disposes of it and the owner of it, and the meaning is: "the share of the Messenger is five, and for the near kin," as in His saying ﴿They ask you about the anfal. Say: the anfal belong to God and the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 1]. The second is that the meaning is: the fifth is spent on the ways of nearness to God, the Exalted. This is the view of the majority. On this view, the waw (and) is superfluous, as in His saying ﴿When they had both submitted and he had thrown him down upon his brow﴾ and ﴿We called out to him﴾ [al-Saffat: 103]. The meaning is: "We called out to him." There are many similar examples.

Section

The scholars agreed that four-fifths of the spoils belong exclusively to the people of war. As for the remaining fifth, how is it divided? There are three opinions on this.

The first is that it is divided into shares for God, for the Messenger, and for those mentioned in the verse. We have already noted that this is a view held by Abu al-Aliya alone, and it requires that it be divided into six shares.

The second is that it is divided into five shares: a share for the Messenger, a share for the near kin, a share for the orphans, a share for the needy, and a share for the wayfarer, according to the apparent sense of the verse. The majority hold this view.

The third is that it is divided into four shares. The share of God, the Mighty and Majestic, and the share of His Messenger go to the near kin, because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not take anything from it. This meaning was transmitted by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas.

[p-360] Section

As for the share of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he used to dispose of it in the ways we have explained. Did it lapse at his death or not? On this there are two opinions.

One is that it did not lapse at his death. This is the view of Ahmad, al-Shafi'i, and others. On how it is to be spent there are two views: one is that it belongs to the caliph after him, said by Qatada; the other is that it is spent on public interests (masalih), the view of Ahmad and al-Shafi'i.

The second is that it lapses at his death, just as the share of the saffi lapses, and so it returns to the total of the spoils. This is the view of Abu Hanifa. As for the near kin, there are three opinions about who they are.

One is that they are all of Quraysh. Ibn Abbas said: "We used to say, 'We are they,' but our people refused us and said, 'All of Quraysh are near kin.'"

The second is that they are the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib. This is the view of Ahmad and al-Shafi'i.

The third is that they are the Banu Hashim alone. This was said by Abu Hanifa. On what basis do they deserve it? On this there are two opinions.

One is by kinship, even if they are wealthy. This is the view of Ahmad and al-Shafi'i.

The second is by poverty, not by lineage alone. This is the view of Abu Hanifa.

The meanings of orphans (yatama), the needy (masakin), and the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil) have already been discussed under [al-Baqara: 177]. For an orphan, four attributes should be considered: the death of the father, even if the mother is still alive; minority, based on the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "There is no orphanhood after reaching maturity (hulm)"; being Muslim, because it is property of the Muslims; and need, because it is set aside for public interests.

[p-361] His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what We sent down upon Our servant on the Day of the Criterion (al-furqan)﴾. This is the Day of Badr, on which God distinguished between truth and falsehood by granting victory to the believers. What was revealed upon him that day was His saying: ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾ [al-Anfal: 1], which was revealed when they disputed about them. So the meaning is: if you have believed in that, then also submit to the command of the Messenger in this matter.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 42:

God's words: ﴿When you were on the near bank of the valley﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "bil-'idwati" (بِالعِدْوَةِ) and "al-'idwati" (العِدْوَةِ), with the ʿayn (ع) vowelled with a kasra in both. Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read both with a damma on the ʿayn. Al-Akhfash said: "Nothing has been heard from the Arabs except the kasra." Tha'lab said: "Rather, the damma is the more common of the two dialects." Ibn al-Sikkit said: "ʿUdwat al-wadi and ʿidwatuhu (عُدْوَةُ الوادِي وعِدْوَتُهُ) mean its side; its plural is ʿidan and ʿudan." Al-dunya (الدُّنْيا) is the feminine of al-adna (the nearer); its opposite is al-quswa (القُصْوى), the feminine of al-aqsa (the farther). Whatever comes among the adjectives in the pattern fa'la from roots with waw, the Arabs convert into ya', as in al-dunya from danawtu (I drew near), and al-ʿulya from ʿalawtu (I rose), because they find the waw heavy after a damma on the first letter. There is no disagreement about this, except that the people of the Hijaz said al-quswa, keeping the waw clear, which is rare; others say al-qusya (القُصْيا). The exegetes said: "When you were on the edge of the valley nearer to Madina, and your enemy was on its far edge, nearer to Makka. The two groups had camped in the valley of Badr in this manner, and the caravan (al-rakb) was Abu Sufyan and his companions."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Whoever puts 'asfala (أَسْفَلَ) in the accusative intends: and the caravan was in a place lower than you. The nominative is also permissible, meaning: and the caravan was lower in its descent than you." Qatada said: "The Muslims were at the upper part of the valley, and the polytheists at its lower part."

In His words: ﴿Had you arranged a meeting, you would have differed about the appointment﴾, there are two opinions.

One: Had you arranged a meeting, then their large number reached you, you would have held back from the appointment. This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

The second: Had you agreed upon a meeting at the place where you met on either side of the valley of Badr, you would have differed about the appointment. This was said by Abu Sulayman. Al-Mawardi said: increase and decrease, or advance and delay, would occur without intending that.

God's words: ﴿But that God might accomplish a matter that was to be done﴾, which is the strengthening of Islam and the humbling of polytheism.

God's words: ﴿That whoever perished might perish after clear proof﴾. Khalaf related from Yahya: "liyuhlaka" (لِيُهْلَكَ), with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the lam.

God's words: ﴿And whoever lived might live after clear proof﴾. Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "man hayya" (مَن حَيَّ) with a single shadda-ed ya'. This is the transmission of Hafs from 'Asim, and Qunbul from Ibn Kathir. Shibl related from Ibn Kathir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim: "hayiya" (حَيِيَ) with two ya's, the first kasra and the second fatha; this is the reading of Nafi'. Whoever reads with two ya's makes them distinct and does not assimilate. Whoever assimilates the ya' of "hayyiya" does so because two letters of the same kind come together. There are two opinions about the meaning of the sentence.

One: that whoever among the polytheists was killed would be killed after a proof, and whoever remained of them would remain after a proof.

The second: that whoever disbelieved would disbelieve after a proof had been established, and whoever believed would believe after a proof.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 43:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When God showed them to you in your dream as few﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions.

The first: that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) saw the army of the polytheists in his dream before they met, as few in number. This was said by Abu Salih, on the authority of Ibn Abbas. Mujahid said: when he informed his companions that he had seen them in his dream as few, that was a reassurance (tathbit) for them. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: the speech is connected to what precedes it, so the meaning is: indeed God is All-Hearing of what your companions say, All-Knowing of what they conceal, when I related to them what you saw in your dream.

The second: "When God showed them to you" with your eye with which you sleep. This was said by al-Hasan. Al-Zajjaj said: many of the grammarians hold this view. Its meaning for them is: "When God showed them to you in the place of your sleep", that is, with your eye; then the place was omitted and sleep was put in its place.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿you would have lost heart﴾, that is, you would have become cowardly and held back from fighting them. Mujahid said: your companions would have lost heart, and they would have seen that in your face.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and you would have disputed about the matter﴾, that is, you would have disagreed about fighting them, and that would have been one of the causes of your defeat. But God protected [you] from disobedience and cowardice.

(p-٣٦٤) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] when He showed them to you as few when you met, and He made them appear few in your eyes﴾. Muqatil said: Allah made true the dream of His Messenger, which he told the believers about, concerning the fewness of their enemy before they met, [that] He would make them few in their eyes at the time of the encounter. Ibn Mas'ud said: They appeared few in our eyes, so much that I said to a man beside me: "Do you think they are seventy?" He said: "I think they are a hundred." Until we seized a man from them and asked him, and he said: "We were a thousand." Abu Salih said, from Ibn 'Abbas: The Muslims considered the polytheists few, and the polytheists considered the Muslims few, so some of them became emboldened against others.

If it is said: what is the benefit of repeating the seeing here, when it was mentioned in His saying: ﴿when Allah showed them to you﴾? Regarding this there are two answers.

One: the first was in a dream, and the second was in wakefulness.

Two: the first was specifically for the Prophet (ﷺ), and the second was for him and his companions.

If it is said: making the believers appear numerous in the eyes of the disbelievers is more fitting, because of its effect of honoring them. In response there are three answers.

First: if they had appeared numerous in their eyes, they would not have advanced against them, so there would have been no fighting; and fighting is the cause of victory, so He made them appear few for that reason.

Second: He made them appear few lest the polytheists prepare fully; then when fighting occurred, the Muslims found them unprepared and gained victory over them.

Third: He made them appear few so that the enemies would charge against them because of their numbers, and the Muslims would overcome them, and that would be a sign for the polytheists and a reminder of the victory of truth.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 45–46:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When you meet a company (fi'ah), then stand firm﴾. The fi'ah is the group.

﴿And remember Allah much﴾. Regarding this there are two statements.

One of them: that it is supplication and seeking victory. The second: the remembrance of Allah in general.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not dispute, lest you lose courage﴾. The mention of dispute (tanazu') and loss of courage (fashal) has already preceded.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and your strength (rih) would depart﴾. Aban narrated it as "wayadhhab" with a ya' and a jazm (jussive). Regarding it there are four statements.

The first: your vigor departs, as Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Suddi said: your zeal and your earnestness. Al-Zajjaj said: your assault and your power.

The second: your victory departs, as said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The third: your dominion is cut off, as said by Abu 'Ubaydah. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said, "the wind of victory blew for him," when he had the dominion; and it is said, "the rih today," meaning the dominion.

The fourth: that it is an actual wind, and victory has never come except by a wind which Allah sends, which strikes the faces of the enemy. From this is his saying, peace be upon him: "I was made victorious by the east wind (al-Saba), and 'Ad were destroyed by the west wind (al-Dabur)." This is the statement of Ibn Zayd and Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 45–46:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When you meet a company (fi'ah), then stand firm﴾. The fi'ah is the group.

﴿And remember Allah much﴾. Regarding this there are two statements.

One of them: that it is supplication and seeking victory. The second: the remembrance of Allah in general.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not dispute, lest you lose courage﴾. The mention of dispute (tanazu') and loss of courage (fashal) has already preceded.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and your strength (rih) would depart﴾. Aban narrated it as "wayadhhab" with a ya' and a jazm (jussive). Regarding it there are four statements.

The first: your vigor departs, as Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Suddi said: your zeal and your earnestness. Al-Zajjaj said: your assault and your power.

The second: your victory departs, as said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The third: your dominion is cut off, as said by Abu 'Ubaydah. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is said, "the wind of victory blew for him," when he had the dominion; and it is said, "the rih today," meaning the dominion.

The fourth: that it is an actual wind, and victory has never come except by a wind which Allah sends, which strikes the faces of the enemy. From this is his saying, peace be upon him: "I was made victorious by the east wind (al-Saba), and 'Ad were destroyed by the west wind (al-Dabur)." This is the statement of Ibn Zayd and Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 47:

﴿And do not be like those who went forth from their homes in insolence and to be seen by people, and who averted [others] from the way of Allah. And Allah is encompassing of what they do.﴾ (p-366)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not be like those who went forth from their homes in insolence﴾. The exegetes said: They are Abu Jahl and those who went out with him from Makkah. They went out to defend their caravan which was with Abu Sufyan, and with them were singing-girls and musical instruments, and they were drinking wine. When Abu Sufyan saw that he had secured what was with him, he wrote to them: "Indeed I have secured your wealth, so return." Abu Jahl said: "By Allah, we will not do so until we reach Badr, and remain there three days, slaughter camels, feed people, serve wine, and the Arabs will hear of us, and they will continue to fear us." So they proceeded to Badr, and the battle occurred; they were given the cups of death instead of wine, and the mourning women wailed over them instead of the singing-girls.

As for *al-bataru* (insolence, exultation), it is transgression in blessings and neglecting to give thanks for them. And *al-riya'* (showing off) is acting for the sake of being seen by people. And *sabil Allah* (the way of Allah) here is: His religion.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when Satan made their deeds appear attractive to them﴾. Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: When Quraysh resolved to march to Badr, they recalled the war between them and Kinanah. Iblis appeared to them in the form of Suraqah ibn Malik al-Mudlaji, who was one of the nobles of Banu Kinanah, and said to them: ﴿No one among the people will overcome you today, and I am your protector against Kinanah bringing you anything you dislike.﴾ So they set out eagerly.

Regarding the meaning of "their deeds" here, there are three opinions.

The first is their polytheism (shirk). The second is their march to Badr. The third is their fighting against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿When the two forces saw each other﴾, meaning they came to a position where each one could see the other. Regarding what is meant by "the two forces," there are two opinions.

One is the force of the Muslims and the force of the polytheists, which is the view of the majority (al-jumhur).

The second is the force of the Muslims and the force of the angels, mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He turned back on his heels﴾. Abu Ubaydah said: he returned the way he had come. Ibn Qutaybah said: he went back backwards (al-qahqara). Ibn al-Sa'ib said: Iblis was in the ranks of the polytheists in the form of Suraqah, holding the hand of al-Harith ibn Hisham. When he saw the angels, he turned back on his heels. Al-Harith said to him: "Are you fleeing without fighting?" He said: ﴿Indeed, I see what you do not see.﴾ When the polytheists were defeated, they said: "Suraqah has routed the people." This reached him, and he said: "By Allah, I did not know of your march until your defeat reached me."

Qatadah said: The promise of Allah was true in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I see what you do not see﴾. It was reported to us that he saw Jibril with the angels, so he knew that he had no power against the angels. The enemy of Allah lied in his saying: ﴿Indeed, I fear Allah﴾. By Allah, he had no fear of Allah, but he knew that he had no strength against them.

Ata' said: its meaning is: "Indeed, I fear that Allah will destroy me."

Ibn al-Anbari said: When he saw the descent of the angels, he feared that the Resurrection had come, which would end his respite, and punishment would befall him. The meaning of "nakasa" is that he returned fleeing in disgrace and humiliation.

They differed regarding His saying: ﴿And Allah is severe in punishment﴾: is it the beginning of a separate statement, or the completion of the account about Iblis? There are two opinions.

(p-367)

The Qur'an, 8:49: ﴿When the hypocrites say﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: They are a group of the people of Madina from the Aws and the Khazraj. As for those in whose hearts is a sickness, there are three opinions concerning them.

The first: they were a group who had professed Islam in Makka, but the polytheists took them out with them on the Day of Badr against their will. When they saw the small number of the Muslims and the large number of the polytheists, they doubted and became hypocrites, and they said: ﴿Their religion has deluded these people﴾. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Sha'bi went to this view along with others. Muqatil counted them and said: they were seven: Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Qays ibn al-Fakih ibn al-Mughira, al-Harith ibn Zam'a, 'Ali ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf, al-'As ibn Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj, al-Walid ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and al-Walid ibn 'Utba ibn Rabi'a.

The second: they are the polytheists, who, when they saw the small number of the Muslims, said: "Their religion has deluded these people." This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan also said so.

The third: they are a people in doubt who did not openly show enmity to the Prophet (ﷺ); this was mentioned by al-Mawardi. The "sickness" here means doubt, and the reference in the words "these people" is to the Muslims. They only said this because they saw the small number of the Muslims, and so they had no doubt that Quraysh would overcome them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 50:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you could see when the angels take the lives of those who disbelieve﴾. Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read "yatawaffa" with a ya'. Ibn 'Amir read "tatawaffa" with two taa'. The exegetes said: it was revealed concerning the group who said, "Their religion has deluded these people." Regarding what is meant by "the angels" there are three opinions.

One: the Angel of Death alone; this was said by Muqatil. The second: the angels of punishment; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. The third: the angels who fought on the Day of Badr; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Regarding His saying: ﴿striking their faces and their backs﴾ there are four opinions.

One: they strike their faces at Badr when they fought, and their backs when they fled. The second: they came to them from before them and from behind them; those in front struck their faces, and those behind struck their backs. The third: they strike their faces and their backs on the Day of Resurrection when they meet them, and their backs when they drive them into the Fire. The fourth: they strike their faces and their backs at death with whips of fire. Is the intended meaning the faces and backs themselves, or what came forward and what turned back of their bodies? On this there are two opinions.

Regarding His saying: ﴿and taste the punishment of the burning﴾ there are two opinions.

One: that it refers to this world; and there is an implied "they say" (yaqulun) in it, so the meaning is: they strike and say, like His saying: ﴿And when Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House, [they said], "Our Lord..."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127], meaning: "and they said." The Nabigha said:

"As if you were one of the camels of the Banu Uqaysh, clinking behind its hind legs with a worn water-skin."

The meaning is: as if you were a camel of the Banu Uqaysh. This is the view of al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda.

The second: that the striking is for them in this world; then when they are brought to the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, its guardians say: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾. This is the view of Muqatil.

(p-370) His words, exalted is He: ﴿That is because of what your hands have put forward﴾, meaning: because of what you earned of the ugly deeds of your actions, ﴿and that Allah is not unjust to the servants﴾. He does not wrong His servants by punishing them for disbelief, even though their disbelief is by His decree, because He is the Owner, so He has the freedom to dispose of His dominion as He wills, and therefore attributing injustice to Him is impossible.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 52:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿As was the case of the people of Pharaoh﴾, meaning: as was their custom (ka-'adatihim). The meaning is: these people denied just as those people denied, so the punishment descended upon them just as it descended upon those. Ibn 'Abbas said: The people of Pharaoh were certain that Musa was a prophet of Allah, yet they denied him; likewise these (people) in regard to Muhammad (ﷺ),

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 53:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is because Allah﴾ meaning: that seizing and punishment is because Allah ﴿would not change a favor He had bestowed upon a people until they change what is in themselves﴾ by ingratitude (kufran) and abandoning thankfulness. Muqatil said: the "people" here refers to the people of Makkah. He fed them after hunger and secured them after fear, then He sent Muhammad (ﷺ) among them, but they did not recognize the One who had bestowed favor upon them, so Allah changed what was with them. As-Suddi said: they denied Muhammad, so Allah transferred (the favor) to the Ansar. Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi said: "al-Qawiy" (the Mighty) means "al-Qadir" (the Capable); whoever is strong in respect of something has power over it. It may also mean the one of complete strength (p-371) who is never overcome by weakness in any state. The created being, even if described as strong, has limited strength, and in some matters it is deficient.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 54:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh and those before them﴾. That is: the people of Makkah denied Muhammad and the Qur'an, just as the people of Pharaoh denied Musa and the Torah, and those before them denied their prophets.

Makki ibn Abi Talib (Makki ibn Abi Talib) said: the kaf in "kada'b" (like the custom of) is in the accusative position, as an adjectival qualifier (na't) of an omitted noun, whose sense is: "We changed what was upon them when they changed, a change like Our custom with the people of Pharaoh." Its parallel is the first verse, except that the first refers to the custom regarding punishment. Its sense is: "We dealt with them in that manner, an action like Our custom with the people of Pharaoh."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So We destroyed them﴾. He means the earlier nations: some of them by the quake (al-raj'fa), and some of them by the wind. Thus We destroyed the disbelievers of Makkah at Badr. Some of them said: by His saying "So We destroyed them" He means those who were destroyed at Badr.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 55:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the worst of living beings in the sight of Allah are those who disbelieve﴾. Abu Salih related from Ibn Abbas: it was revealed concerning the Banu Qurayza of the Jews, among them Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions.

(p-372)

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those with whom you made a covenant﴾. Regarding "min" (from) there are four opinions.

The first is that it is a *ṣilah* (a redundant particle that adds no meaning), and the meaning is: "Those with whom you made a covenant."

The second is that it is for *tab'īḍ* (partitive, meaning "some of"). Then the meaning is: "Indeed the worst of the beasts are the disbelievers, and the worst of them are those with whom you made a covenant and who broke it."

The third is that it has the meaning of *ma'a* (with). Then the meaning is: "You made a covenant with them."

The fourth is that it is included because the covenant was taken from them.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Then they break their covenant every time﴾, meaning: whenever you make a covenant with them, they break it.

Regarding His statement: ﴿and they do not fear﴾, there are two opinions.

One is: they do not fear breaking the covenant. The other is: they do not fear God in breaking the covenant.

The exegetes (*mufassirūn*) said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had made a covenant with the Jews of Banu Qurayzah that they would not wage war against him and would not assist anyone against him. They broke the covenant and assisted the idolaters of Makkah against him with weapons. Then they said, 'We forgot and we erred.' Then they made a second covenant with him, and they broke it and colluded with the disbelievers on the Day of the Trench (*Khandaq*). Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf wrote to Makkah agreeing with them to oppose the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 57:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So if you overcome them in war﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: its meaning (majaz) is: "If you overcome them." According to this view, "ma" (in "fa-imma") is superfluous (za'ida). The explanation of "fa-imma" has already passed in (al-Baqarah: 38). Ibn Qutayba said: the meaning of "tathqafannahum" is "you gain mastery over them" (tazfar bihim). ﴿Then disperse those behind them﴾, i.e., deal with them with such a punishment and exemplary chastisement that those behind them of your enemies will be scattered by it. He said: it is also said: "sharrid bihim," meaning "sammi' bihim" (make an example of them), in the dialect of Quraysh. The poet said:

I roam through the valleys every day, fearing that Hakim may make me an example (yashrud bi).

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Nakkil bihim taknilan" (inflict upon them a punishment that deters others among those who break the covenant), so that perhaps they will remember the punishment and not break the covenant.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 58:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people﴾. The exegetes said: "Fear" here means "knowledge," and the meaning is: if you know of a people with whom you have a treaty that they are treacherous, and treachery is the breaking of a covenant. Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the Banu Qurayza.

Regarding His saying: ﴿then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms﴾ there are four opinions.

The first: then inform them of your breaking of the covenant, so that you and they are equal in knowledge of the breach. This is the view of most scholars, and it was chosen by al-Farra' (al-Farra', the grammarian and exegete) and Ibn Qutayba (Ibn Qutayba, the scholar of language and hadith), and Abu 'Ubayda (Abu 'Ubayda, the philologist).

The second: then throw it back to them openly, not secretly. al-Farra' also mentioned this, along with others.

The third: then throw it back to them with deliberation (or in a measured way). This was said by al-Walid ibn Muslim.

The fourth: then throw it back to them on the basis of justice, without injustice. They cited the verse of poetry:

"Strike the faces of the treacherous enemies until they respond to you with equity."

Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi mentioned this.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 59:

His saying, may He be exalted: "Let not those who disbelieved think that they have escaped (sabaqu)." Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, from ʿĀṣim, recited "وَلا تَحْسَبْنَّ" (wa-lā taḥsabanna) with the taʾ (ta) and a kasra on the sin, except that ʿĀṣim put a fatha on the sin. Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, and Ḥafṣ, from ʿĀṣim, recited it with the yaʾ (ya) and a fatha on the sin. (Qira'at: the canonical variant readings of the Qur'an.)

Regarding "those who disbelieved" (al-kāfirīn) here, there are two opinions.

The first: all the disbelievers. This was said by Abu Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second: they are those who fled on the day of Badr. This was mentioned by Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim al-Naḥwī and others. "Sabaqū" means "escaped" (fātū). Ibn al-Anbārī said: The reason is that they feared a destruction that would befall them at some time; then, when they were spared from it, it was said: "Do not think that they have escaped by their safety now, for they will not escape us (lā yuʿjizūnā)," meaning: they will not elude us in the times they face in the future.

His saying, may He be exalted: "Indeed they will not escape" (innahum lā yuʿjizūn). The majority recited the alif with a kasra (inna). Ibn ʿĀmir recited it with a fatha (annahum). On his recitation there is an objection. Someone may say: if he recited "yaḥsabanna" with the yaʾ and recited "annahum" with the fatha, then he has affirmed that they will not escape; and when they know that they will not escape, they are not to be blamed. Ibn al-Anbārī answered this, saying: the meaning is: "Let not those who disbelieved think that they have escaped": let them not think that they will escape; and "wa-lā" (and not) is an extra, emphasising particle (zāʾidah muʾakkidah). Abu ʿAlī said: the meaning is: let not those who disbelieved think that they themselves have escaped, or that their fathers have escaped, because they will not be beyond reach, so they will be recompensed for their disbelief.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 60:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you can of power﴾, concerning the meaning of "power" (quwwah) there are four opinions.

The first: it is archery (al-ramy). This was narrated by ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmir from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Al-Hakam ibn Abان said: it is arrows (al-nubl). The second: male horses (dhukur al-khayl), said by ʿIkrimah. The third: weapons (al-silah), said by al-Suddi and Ibn Qutaybah. The fourth: it is everything by which one is strengthened for fighting the enemy, of the implements of jihad.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and from the tethering of horses﴾, meaning tying them and keeping them for raiding; and it is general to males and females according to the view of the majority. ʿIkrimah used to say: what is meant by His saying "and from the tethering of horses" is their females.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿by which you terrify﴾. Ruways and ʿAbd al-Warith related "turhibun" with a fatha on the ra' and a shaddah on the ha', meaning: you frighten and strike terror into, by it, the enemy of Allah and your enemy, and they are the polytheists of Makkah and the disbelievers of the Arabs.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and others besides them﴾, meaning besides the disbelievers of the Arabs. They differed concerning them on five opinions.

The first: they are the jinn. It was reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "They are the jinn, and indeed Satan does not harm anyone in whose house there is an old horse." The second: they are the Banu Qurayzah, said by Mujahid. The third: the people of Persia, said by al-Suddi. The fourth: the hypocrites, said by Ibn Zayd. The fifth: the Jews, said by Muqatil.

If they say: why did He say "lahā" (to it) and not "ilayhā" (towards it)?

The answer: the lam (ل) and "ila" (إلى, towards) each may stand in for the other. Regarding those intended by this verse there are two opinions.

The first: the polytheists, and that it was abrogated by the verse of the sword (āyat al-sayf).

The second: the People of the Book.

If it is said that it was revealed concerning leaving off fighting them when they offered the jizya (poll tax) and upheld the terms of the dhimma (protected status), then it is muhkam (clear, not abrogated).

And if it is said that it was revealed concerning a truce with them without jizya, then abrogation applies to it by the verse of the jizya.

Allah's statement: ﴿And if they intend﴾ Muqatil said: it means the Jews of Banu Qurayzah (﴿to deceive you﴾) through reconciliation, so that you would hold back from them, until the polytheists of the Arabs come and aid them against you. (﴿Then indeed Allah is sufficient for you﴾). Al-Zajjaj said: the one who takes charge of your sufficiency is Allah. ﴿It is He who supported you﴾, meaning: He strengthened you. Muqatil said: He strengthened you with His help and with the believers from the Ansar on the Day of Badr.

Allah's statement: ﴿And He joined their hearts together﴾, meaning the Aws and the Khazraj, who are the Ansar. There was enmity between them in the Jahiliyyah, and Allah joined them together through Islam. This is among the most wondrous of the verses, because they were people of intense pride (anafah, a sense of honor and self-regard). If a man slapped another man, his tribe would fight on his behalf until they avenged his blood, and Islam led them to the point where a man would kill his own son and his own father.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 64:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Sufficient for you is Allah, and for those who follow you﴾ — there are two opinions concerning it.

The first: "Sufficient for you is Allah, and sufficient for those who follow you." This is the view of Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Zayd, Muqatil, and most scholars held it.

The second: "Sufficient for you is Allah and your followers." This was said by Mujahid. It is also reported from al-Sha'bi as being like the two opinions.

Al-Farra' (tafsir: Qur'anic exegesis; here, the grammarian Abu Zakariyya al-Farra') and al-Zajjaj (the grammarian Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj) permitted both readings. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Thirty-nine people had embraced Islam with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then Umar embraced Islam, and they became forty, and this verse was revealed." Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: "This is not preserved, and the surah is Medinan by consensus, and the first opinion is more sound."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 65–66:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O Prophet, urge the believers to fight﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: its interpretation is "urging them" (hathth-hum). The meaning of tahrid (urging) in the language is that one urges a person toward a thing with such urging that he knows that, if he holds back from it, he will be ruined (haarid). A haarid is one who has come close to destruction.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If there are twenty of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾. The wording of this statement is in the form of a report, but its meaning is a command, and what is intended is: "Let them fight two hundred." This was an obligation at the beginning of the matter, and then it was abrogated (nusikha) by His saying: ﴿Now Allah has lightened your burden﴾. So it was made obligatory upon the man to stand firm against two men; if they increased in number, it became permissible for him to flee. Mujahid said: this strictness was at the Battle of Badr.

The reciters agreed on His saying ﴿in-yakun min-kum﴾ (if there are among you), reading "yakun" with a ya'. They differed concerning His saying ﴿wa-in yakun min-kum mi'atun yaghlibu alfan﴾ (and if there are among you one hundred, they will overcome a thousand) and concerning His saying (fa-in takun min-kum mi'atun sabirah) (so if there are among you one hundred steadfast). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Ibn 'Amir read both with ta' (takun). 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read both with ya' (yakun). Abu 'Amr read "yakun min-kum mi'atun yaghlibu" with ya', and "fa-in takun min-kum mi'atun sabirah" with ta'. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever uses the feminine form does so because of the word mi'ah (hundred); whoever uses the masculine does so because mi'ah refers to a masculine number. Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads with ya' does so because the masculine is intended, as shown by His saying "yaghlibu"; likewise the steadfast hundred are men, so they read it with ya' for the sake of the masculine sense. As for Abu 'Amr, when he saw the attribute of mi'ah in the feminine, in His saying "sabirah", he made the verb feminine; and when he saw "yaghlibu" in the masculine, he made it masculine.

The meaning of the statement is: if there are among you twenty steadfast ones who hold firm at the encounter, they will overcome two hundred, because the believers seek reward for their deeds, while the people of polytheism fight without seeking reward or pursuing merit. When the believers meet them in battle, they do not hold firm; and that is the meaning of His saying: ﴿for they are a people who do not understand﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: "wa-'alima (and He knows) ..." Al-Mufaddal related "wa-'ulima" with a damma on the 'ayn, "anna fi-kum da'fan" with a damma on the dad. 'Asim and Hamzah read it with a fatha on the dad. Their difference regarding (al-Rum: 54) is similar. Al-Farra' said: the damma is the dialect of Quraysh, and the fatha is the dialect of Tamim. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning in both readings is one; it is said "huwa al-da'f" and "al-du'f," "al-makth" and "al-mukth," "al-faqr" and "al-fuqr," and in the language there are many examples of the pattern fa'l and fu'l, with one meaning. Abu Ja'far read "wa-'alima anna fi-kum du'afa'" in the pattern fa'ala'. As for His saying ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, it is an informing that victory does not occur except by His will.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 67:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he has inflicted a massacre upon the land.﴾ Muslim related in his separate collection, from the hadith of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "When Allah defeated the polytheists on the day of Badr, and seventy of them were killed and seventy were taken captive, the Prophet (ﷺ) consulted Abu Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿAli. Abu Bakr said: 'O Prophet of Allah, these are our paternal cousins, kinsmen and brothers. I think you should take ransom from them, so that what we take from them will be a strength for us against the disbelievers, and perhaps Allah will guide them and they will become a support for us.' The Messenger of Allah said: 'What do you think, O son of al-Khattab?' I said: 'By Allah, I do not see what Abu Bakr sees, but I think you should let me have so-and-so, a relative of ʿUmar, so that I may strike his neck, and let ʿAli have ʿAqil so that he may strike his neck, and let Hamza have his brother so-and-so so that he may strike his neck, until Allah knows that there is no leniency in our hearts toward the polytheists. These are their chieftains, their leaders and their commanders.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) inclined to what Abu Bakr said, and did not incline to what I said, so he took the ransom from them. When the next day came, I went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and found him sitting with Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and both of them were weeping. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, tell me what makes you and your companion weep. If I find a reason to weep I will weep, and if I do not find one I will feign weeping.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'I weep for what your companions proposed to me regarding the ransom. Your punishment was presented to me [as close] as this tree'—a nearby tree—and Allah revealed: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives…﴾ until His saying: '…great.'"

And it is related from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "When ʿUmar advised their execution and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) accepted ransom from them, Allah revealed: 'It is not for a Prophet…' until His saying: '…lawful and good.' Then the Prophet (ﷺ) met ʿUmar and said: 'Calamity almost befell us because of your opposition.'"

As for "al-asra" (captives), it is the plural of "asir" (captive), which we have mentioned in (al-Baqarah: 85). The majority read "an yakuna" with the ya', because "al-asra" is masculine. Abu ʿAmr read "an takuna" with the ta'. Abu ʿAli said: it was made feminine in agreement with the wording "al-asra," since "al-asra," although what is meant by it is the masculine, men, is feminine in wording. Most readers read "asra," and likewise "li-man fi aydikum mina al-asra" (in the verse of al-Anfal). Abu Jaʿfar and al-Mufaddal read "asara" in both places, and Abu ʿAmr and Aban agreed with them in the second. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-ithkhan" in everything means the strength and intensity of a thing. It is said: "The illness has inflicted him (athkhanahu)" when its strength over him has become intense. The meaning is: until he goes to excess in killing his enemies. It is also possible that the meaning is: until he becomes firmly established in the land. The exegetes said: the meaning of the verse is: it is not for a Prophet to hold a disbeliever whom he has power over, for ransom or for release, before inflicting a massacre upon the land. The battle of Badr was the first fight that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fought, and he had not yet inflicted a massacre upon the land.

﴿You desire the goods of this world﴾, which is wealth. The Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) had ransomed that day at four thousand each, four thousand each. Regarding His saying: ﴿but Allah desires the Hereafter﴾ there are two views.

One: He desires for you the Garden; this is said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: He desires the action that brings the reward of the Hereafter; this is mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Section

It has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid, among others, that this verse is abrogated by His saying: ﴿Then either grace afterwards or ransom﴾ [Muhammad: 4]. There is no basis for abrogation here, because the battle of Badr took place while the Muslims were few; when they increased and their authority became strong, the other verse was revealed. This is shown by His saying: ﴿until he has inflicted a massacre upon the land﴾.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verse 68:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that preceded﴾, has five interpretations.

The first: Had it not been that Allah had written in the Mother of the Book (Umm al-Kitab, the Preserved Tablet) that He would make the spoils lawful for you, He would have touched you with a great punishment for what you hastened to take of the booty and the ransom on the day of Badr, before you were commanded to do so. This interpretation was related by Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas, and Muqatil said likewise. Abu Hurayrah said: Some of the Muslims hastened and took the spoils, so the verse was revealed.

The second: Had it not been a decree from Allah that preceded, that He does not punish whoever commits a sin in ignorance, you would have been punished. This interpretation was related by Ata from Ibn Abbas, and by Ibn Jurayj from Mujahid. Ibn Ishaq said: It preceded that I would not punish except after a prohibition, and He had not forbidden them.

The third: Had it not been for what had preceded concerning the people of Badr, that Allah would not punish them, you would have been punished. This was said by al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, and Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid.

The fourth: Had it not been a decree from Allah that preceded, that He forgives whoever commits sins and then realizes what is upon him and repents. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The fifth: Had it not been for the Qur'an, which required the forgiveness of minor sins, you would have been punished. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Accordingly, two views arise concerning the "Book."

One of them: that it is a literally written book. Within this there are two views: one, that it is what Allah wrote on the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz); and the other, that it is the Qur'an.

The second: that it means decree (al-qada').

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verses 69–70:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So eat of what you have taken as booty, lawful and good﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the fa' (fa, "so") is for the consequence (jaza'). The meaning is: "I have made the ransom (fida') lawful for you, so eat." The word ḥalāl ("lawful") is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). Muqatil said: Indeed Allah is Forgiving of what you took from the spoils before it was made lawful, Merciful to you in that He made it lawful for you.

"The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) appointed ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and Khabbab ibn al-Aratt over the collection on the day of Badr, and the Prophet (ﷺ) divided it at Medina, and he set out with the captives, among whom were al-ʿAbbas, ʿAqil, and Nawfal ibn al-Harith ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib. With al-ʿAbbas on that day were twenty ounces of gold, but it was not counted toward his ransom, and he was required to ransom his two nephews, so he paid on their behalf eighty ounces of gold. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Increase the ransom upon al-ʿAbbas,' so they took from him eighty ounces, while the ransom of each captive was forty ounces. Al-ʿAbbas said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'You have left me, as long as I live, to beg Quraysh with my hand.' He said to him: 'Where is the gold that you left with Umm al-Fadl?' He said: 'What gold?' He said: 'You said to her: I do not know what may befall me in this venture of mine; if some misfortune happens to me, then it is yours and your children's.' He said: 'Nephew, who informed you?' He said: 'Allah informed me.' Al-ʿAbbas said: 'I testify that you are truthful, and I did not know before today that you were the Messenger of Allah'; and he commanded his two nephews, and they embraced Islam. And concerning them was revealed: ﴿Say to those in your hands of the captives...﴾ the verse."

Al-ʿAwfi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed concerning all who were taken captive on the day of Badr. Ibn Zayd said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent, men came to him and said: 'Were it not that we fear these people, we would embrace Islam, but we bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah.' When the day of Badr came, the polytheists said: 'None of you shall hold back from us except that we will demolish his house and seize his property.' So those people went out, and a group of them was killed and a group was taken captive. As for those who were killed, they are those concerning whom Allah said: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ [al-Nahl: 28]. As for those who were taken captive, they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you know that we used to bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah, and we only went out with these people out of fear of them.' That is His saying: ﴿Say to those in your hands of the captives﴾ up to His saying ﴿Knowing, Wise﴾."

As for His saying: ﴿If Allah knows any good in your hearts﴾, its meaning is Islam and sincerity. ﴿He will give you better than what was taken from you﴾ — referring to the ransom. There are two views concerning it. One: more than what was taken from you. The second: lawful and better.

And al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read "mimma ukhidha minkum" with a fatḥah on the kha', referring to Allah the Exalted.

Concerning His saying: ﴿And He will forgive you﴾ there are two views.

One: He will forgive you your disbelief and your fighting against the Messenger of Allah; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: He will forgive you your going out with the polytheists; this was said by Ibn Zayd in the completion of his first statement.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 8, verses 69–70:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So eat of what you have taken as booty, lawful and good﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the fa' (fa, "so") is for the consequence (jaza'). The meaning is: "I have made the ransom (fida') lawful for you, so eat." The word ḥalāl ("lawful") is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). Muqatil said: Indeed Allah is Forgiving of what you took from the spoils before it was made lawful, Merciful to you in that He made it lawful for you.

"The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) appointed ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and Khabbab ibn al-Aratt over the collection on the day of Badr, and the Prophet (ﷺ) divided it at Medina, and he set out with the captives, among whom were al-ʿAbbas, ʿAqil, and Nawfal ibn al-Harith ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib. With al-ʿAbbas on that day were twenty ounces of gold, but it was not counted toward his ransom, and he was required to ransom his two nephews, so he paid on their behalf eighty ounces of gold. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Increase the ransom upon al-ʿAbbas,' so they took from him eighty ounces, while the ransom of each captive was forty ounces. Al-ʿAbbas said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'You have left me, as long as I live, to beg Quraysh with my hand.' He said to him: 'Where is the gold that you left with Umm al-Fadl?' He said: 'What gold?' He said: 'You said to her: I do not know what may befall me in this venture of mine; if some misfortune happens to me, then it is yours and your children's.' He said: 'Nephew, who informed you?' He said: 'Allah informed me.' Al-ʿAbbas said: 'I testify that you are truthful, and I did not know before today that you were the Messenger of Allah'; and he commanded his two nephews, and they embraced Islam. And concerning them was revealed: ﴿Say to those in your hands of the captives...﴾ the verse."

Al-ʿAwfi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed concerning all who were taken captive on the day of Badr. Ibn Zayd said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent, men came to him and said: 'Were it not that we fear these people, we would embrace Islam, but we bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah.' When the day of Badr came, the polytheists said: 'None of you shall hold back from us except that we will demolish his house and seize his property.' So those people went out, and a group of them was killed and a group was taken captive. As for those who were killed, they are those concerning whom Allah said: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ [al-Nahl: 28]. As for those who were taken captive, they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you know that we used to bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah, and we only went out with these people out of fear of them.' That is His saying: ﴿Say to those in your hands of the captives﴾ up to His saying ﴿Knowing, Wise﴾."
